chapter.title: Sun Common SCSI Architecture Version 3 (SCSAv3)
chapter.para: This chapter describes the modern configuration and device-management interfaces commonly associated with the third version of the Sun Common SCSI Architecture (SCSAv3). These interfaces extend the established SCSA command transport model described in . They do not replace the scsi_pkt9S transport contract between target drivers and HBA drivers.
This chapter is provisional. It is separate from so that the modern interfaces can be described coherently while the eventual organization of the SCSA material is decided.

sect1.title: Relationship to Traditional SCSA
sect1.para: Traditional SCSA documentation describes an HBA transport using small integer target and logical-unit addresses. An HBA can clone its transport structure for each target when it needs per-target state or a more complex private address. Device configuration is based on probing possible target and logical-unit addresses. Current interfaces call this the SCSI Parallel Interface (SPI) addressing model.
The modern model retains the transport entry points but adds framework support for more complex topologies and dynamic discovery. Its principal features are:

listitem.para: separate initiator-port (iport) device nodes below the HBA;
string unit addresses and per-device HBA-private state;
framework-managed maps of iports and targets;
dynamic creation and removal of device-tree nodes; and
packet completion through SCSA so that the framework can observe events such as changes in logical-unit configuration.

sect1.para: Not every driver uses every modern interface. For example, a driver can use iport nodes while retaining cloned transport structures. Such combinations are useful for existing drivers, but new SAS HBA drivers should normally use the iport and complex-addressing model described here.

sect1.title: HBA and Initiator-Port (iport) Topology
sect1.para: The modern model separates controller-wide HBA state from SCSI iport state. The top-level HBA node represents resources associated with the controller, such as register mappings and interrupts. Its SCSI-facing children are iports. Each iport represents a collection of attached devices and has its own scsi_hba_tran9S structure.

An iport is a child of the HBA node but binds to the same driver. Creation of an iport therefore causes the driver's attach9E entry point to be called for the iport node. Removal causes its detach9E entry point to be called. The driver distinguishes a top-level HBA attachment from an iport attachment with scsi_hba_iport_unit_address9F, which returns NULL for the top-level HBA.

The SCSI_HBA_HBA flag to scsi_hba_attach_setup9F declares that all direct SCSI-facing children of the HBA node are iports. A driver whose HBA node acts both as an initiator and as the parent of iports must not set this flag.

sect2.title: Static Initiator-Ports (iports)
sect2.para: A driver with a fixed set of iports registers each port with scsi_hba_iport_register9F. An iport need not correspond directly to a physical connector. For example, a controller that presents both firmware-managed logical devices and physical devices can provide separate logical and physical iports.

sect2.title: Dynamic Initiator-Ports (iports)
sect2.para: A driver whose iports appear and disappear dynamically uses an iport map. SAS drivers can also use a phy map to group physical lanes into ports. Changes in the phy map can then cause corresponding entries to be added to or removed from the iport map. The framework creates or removes iport nodes and invokes the driver's normal attachment entry points.
See iport9 and scsi_hba_iportmap_create9F for the iport-map and phy-map interfaces.
The current framework implementation processes iport-map and phy-map configuration serially. This differs from target maps, which can configure or unconfigure different target addresses concurrently.

sect1.title: Complex Addressing and Per-Device State
sect1.para: The traditional scsi_address9S representation contains integer a_target and a_lun fields. These fields are insufficient for transports whose addresses contain values such as worldwide names or other transport-specific components.

An HBA selects complex addressing by passing SCSI_HBA_ADDR_COMPLEX to scsi_hba_attach_setup9F. The HBA must then treat scsi_address9S as opaque except for its transport pointer. It obtains the corresponding scsi_device9S with scsi_address_device9F and obtains the device's string unit address with scsi_device_unit_address9F.

During tran_tgt_init9E, the HBA can translate the unit address and its properties into a private representation. It associates that state with the scsi_device by calling scsi_device_hba_private_set9F. Other transport entry points retrieve the state with scsi_device_hba_private_get9F. The HBA releases the state during tran_tgt_free9E.
This model replaces the need to clone scsi_hba_tran solely to obtain tran_tgt_private and tran_sd. SCSI_HBA_TRAN_CLONE remains supported for compatibility but is deprecated for new drivers.

sect1.title: Target Discovery
sect1.para: A target map represents the SCSI and SCSI Management Protocol (SMP) targets visible through an initiator-port (iport). The HBA reports its observations to the map, and the SCSA framework performs the corresponding device-tree configuration and unconfiguration after the reported topology has stabilized. A target map is created on an iport, not on the top-level HBA node.

sect2.title: Reporting Target Observations
sect2.para: Target maps support two reporting modes:

listitem.para: The driver brackets a complete observation with scsi_hba_tgtmap_set_begin9F and scsi_hba_tgtmap_set_end9F, adding each observed address with scsi_hba_tgtmap_set_add9F. The framework determines which addresses were added and removed. This mode is appropriate when individual hardware notifications can be lost.
The driver reports reliable individual additions and removals with scsi_hba_tgtmap_tgt_add9F and scsi_hba_tgtmap_tgt_remove9F.

sect2.para: When it creates a target map, a driver specifies a stabilization interval and an initial-enumeration synchronization interval.

sect2.title: Target Activation and Deactivation Callbacks
sect2.para: A driver can supply optional activation and deactivation callbacks when it calls scsi_hba_tgtmap_create9F. It can also supply a private value that SCSA passes to both callbacks.

The activation callback runs asynchronously after the driver reports a new target address and before a target driver binds to that address. The callback receives the address, target type, and a pointer to the target's private value. It can replace that value with state that SCSA will pass to the later deactivation callback.

The deactivation callback normally runs after the target driver has detached. It can also run when device configuration fails or when an address is added and removed before it stabilizes. Its reason argument is one of:

listitem.para: The target is no longer reported.
Configuration of the target failed. Returning B_TRUE requests another discovery attempt, but does not guarantee that one will occur. A driver should otherwise return B_FALSE.
The target was added and removed during the stabilization interval.

sect2.para: The current target-map implementation can invoke activation or deactivation callbacks for different target addresses concurrently. A driver must synchronize access to shared HBA or iport state and must not assume that callbacks for separate addresses are serialized.

sect2.title: Target-Map Teardown
sect2.para: scsi_hba_tgtmap_destroy9F stops new reports and waits for stabilization and map-owned configuration, unconfiguration, and callback work. It deactivates all remaining targets before it returns. The driver must prevent other threads from using the map concurrently with destruction or retaining the map handle after destruction frees it.

sect2.title: Logical-Unit Scanning
sect2.para: The scsi_hba_tgtmap_scan_luns9F function requests framework-managed discovery of the logical units associated with a target. The framework issues REPORT LUNS and configures newly reported logical units while removing logical units that are no longer reported.

sect2.title: Self-Identifying HBA Drivers
sect2.para: An HBA that discovers and dynamically creates its SCSI children is self-identifying. Such a driver can be installed in the scsi-self-identifying driver class. This allows target drivers to provide a common configuration stub rather than naming every self-identifying parent driver individually.

sect1.title: Packet Allocation and Completion
sect1.para: The modern configuration model continues to use scsi_pkt9S and the traditional transport entry points. Two newer packet-interface families are important to current HBA drivers but are not unique to SCSAv3.

sect2.title: Framework-Managed Packet and DMA Allocation
sect2.para: An HBA can implement tran_setup_pkt9E and tran_teardown_pkt9E instead of implementing the traditional tran_init_pkt, tran_destroy_pkt, tran_dmafree, and tran_sync_pkt operations. SCSA then manages the packet cache, DMA allocation, and DMA breakup, while the HBA initializes its private packet state and programs the DMA cookies supplied in the packet.

sect2.title: Framework-Observed Completion
sect2.para: After filling in the packet's completion information, a current HBA driver calls scsi_hba_pkt_comp9F instead of invoking pkt_comp directly. Use of scsi_hba_pkt_comp is mandatory for an HBA that implements tran_setup_pkt. It also allows SCSA to observe sense data that indicates a change in the reported logical units of a target.

The target driver's completion callback can occur after scsi_hba_pkt_comp returns and can execute on another thread or CPU. An HBA must not depend on direct, synchronous transfer of control to the target driver's callback.

sect1.title: MPxIO Paths and Device Properties
sect1.para: For an HBA participating in MPxIO, each physical initiator-port (iport) is a separate physical HCI transport. A path through that transport is distinct from the identity of the device reached through the path. The scsi_device_prop_* interfaces let an HBA access or update properties associated with either the device or the path without depending on private multipathing data structures.

This distinction matters when interpreting unit-address and transport properties during tran_tgt_init. A complete description of MPxIO policy and virtual-HCI operation is outside the scope of this chapter.

sect1.title: Choosing an Interface Model
sect1.para: Existing drivers can combine traditional and modern mechanisms, and such combinations remain supported. Documentation and new-driver design should nevertheless keep the following distinctions clear:

listitem.para: SCSI_HBA_ADDR_COMPLEX replaces cloned transports as the preferred way to represent complex addresses and maintain per-device HBA state.
SCSI_HBA_HBA describes the relationship between an HBA node and its initiator-port (iport) children; it does not by itself select an address representation.
Static iport registration and dynamic iport maps are alternative ways to describe the set of iports.
Target maps replace legacy target enumeration for drivers that use framework-managed discovery.
tran_setup_pkt is an alternative packet and DMA allocation model, not a prerequisite for using iports or complex addressing.

sect1.para: For new SAS HBA drivers, scsi_hba_attach_setup9F recommends the combination of SCSI_HBA_HBA and SCSI_HBA_ADDR_COMPLEX. See iport9 for the current overview of the iport, phy-map, iport-map, and target-map interfaces.

listitem.para: PSARC/2008/675, SCSI_HBA_ADDR_COMPLEX SCSA Data Structure Linkage introduces complex addressing and per-device HBA-private state.
PSARC/2008/337, scsi-self-identifying introduces the driver class used by SCSA nexus drivers that dynamically create child nodes.
PSARC/2009/125, scsi_device Property Interfaces defines interfaces for device and path properties and unit-address retrieval.
PSARC/2009/033, scsi_hba_pkt_comp(9F) introduces framework-observed packet completion.
PSARC/2005/680, New scsi_hba_tran Entry Points introduces framework-managed packet allocation.
PSARC/2006/240, SCSA DMA Enhancement extends framework-managed packet allocation to DMA allocation and breakup.
